points: Reverse osmosis unit run at a transmembrane pressure of 15 bar on the tested feed water.
Opening permeate flux of 42 litres per square metre per hour, with a steep early decline and a slower later decline.
Flux reached 31 litres per square metre per hour at 30 days, a decline of 26 percent from the opening value.
Flux values are means over 6 membrane elements; the spread at the end of the trial was 2.4 litres per square metre per hour.
Citric acid cleaning restored flux to 38 litres per square metre per hour; a residual loss against the opening value remained.
definitions: permeate flux = volume of permeate passing through a unit of membrane area in a unit of time
transmembrane pressure = feed-side pressure minus permeate-side pressure
spread of a flux value = standard deviation of the membrane element values at a fixed sampling time
limits: Claims are bound to the tested feed water and the tested pressure.
prose:
Permeate flux decline in the reverse osmosis unit followed two stages across the trial. Permeate flux, the volume of permeate passing through a unit of membrane area in a unit of time, opened the trial at 42 litres per square metre per hour. Transmembrane pressure, the feed-side pressure minus the permeate-side pressure, held at 15 bar throughout the run. Flux fell steeply across the opening days of operation and then settled into a slower decline as deposits accumulated on the membrane surface. The slower stage carried flux to 31 litres per square metre per hour at 30 days. The decline from the opening value reached 26 percent at that point, and the decline curve flattened as the fouling layer compacted under pressure. Each flux value is the mean of 6 membrane elements sampled from the pressure vessel, and the spread of the flux values at the end of the trial was 2.4 litres per square metre per hour. The spread of a flux value is the standard deviation of the membrane element values at a fixed sampling time, and the spread grew as the fouling layer thickened unevenly across the vessel.

Chemical cleaning with a citric acid solution restored part of the lost flux. Flux after cleaning stood at 38 litres per square metre per hour, and the recovered share points to a fouling layer that is partly reversible under the cleaning conditions applied. A residual loss against the opening value remained after cleaning. The residual loss is consistent with material bound tightly to the membrane surface, in pores that the cleaning solution reaches poorly. The two-stage pattern and the partial recovery held for the tested feed water at the tested pressure, and claims for other feed waters or higher pressures stand outside the tested range. Element-to-element variation tracked the deposit pattern seen at the vessel inlet, where the feed distributor leaves a heavier deposit on the elements nearest the inlet ports.

points: Methane yield of the co-digestion mixture reached 0.34 cubic metres per kilogram of volatile solids added.
The food-waste baseline, digested alone under the same conditions, gave 0.28 cubic metres per kilogram; the mixture yield stands 21 percent above the baseline.
Digesters ran at 37 degrees Celsius with a retention time of 25 days.
Organic loading rate held at 2.5 kilograms per cubic metre per day.
Methane content of the biogas averaged 62 percent across the trial.
Yield values are means over 4 digesters run in parallel; the spread of the yield values was 0.02 cubic metres per kilogram.
definitions: methane yield = volume of methane produced per kilogram of volatile solids added
volatile solids = fraction of the feed mass lost on ignition
organic loading rate = mass of volatile solids fed per cubic metre of digester volume per day
spread of a yield value = standard deviation of the digester values within a sampling round
limits: Claims are bound to the tested mixture and the tested temperature.
prose:
Biogas production from the co-digestion mixture held steady across the trial, and methane yield exceeded the food-waste baseline at every sampling round. Methane yield, the volume of methane produced per kilogram of volatile solids added, reached 0.34 cubic metres per kilogram for the mixture. The food-waste baseline, digested alone under the same conditions, gave 0.28 cubic metres per kilogram. The mixture yield stands 21 percent above the baseline value. Volatile solids are the fraction of the feed mass lost on ignition, and the yield denominator is fixed at the point of feeding, before any digestion takes place. The digesters ran at 37 degrees Celsius with a retention time of 25 days, and feeding followed the same daily schedule in every vessel. Organic loading rate, the mass of volatile solids fed per cubic metre of digester volume per day, held at 2.5 kilograms per cubic metre per day across the trial. Methane content of the biogas averaged 62 percent, with the balance made up mainly of carbon dioxide and water vapour.

Each yield value is the mean of 4 digesters run in parallel, and the spread of the yield values was 0.02 cubic metres per kilogram. The spread of a yield value is the standard deviation of the digester values within a sampling round. The higher yield from the mixture is consistent with a nutrient balance that the food waste alone does not supply, and the steady methane content points to a stable microbial community under the tested loading. Claims are bound to the tested mixture and the tested temperature, and performance at other mixture compositions stands outside the trial. Gas production held through each feeding cycle without the foaming or souring that marks an overloaded digester, and the digestate left the vessels with a stable consistency across the trial period. The mixture vessels and the baseline vessels shared the same inoculum at start-up, drawn from a single working digester on the site.

points: Inlet air temperature of 180 degrees Celsius with an outlet air temperature of 85 degrees Celsius.
Feed solids content held at 40 percent throughout the runs.
Powder moisture reached 3.2 percent against a specification limit of 4.0 percent.
At an inlet air temperature of 160 degrees Celsius, powder moisture stood at 4.6 percent.
Production rate held at 250 kilograms per hour.
Moisture values are means over 12 batches; the spread of the batch values was 0.3 percent.
definitions: outlet moisture = mass of water per unit mass of wet powder leaving the dryer, expressed as a percentage
specification limit = maximum powder moisture accepted for the product grade under test
spread of a moisture value = standard deviation of the batch values within a run set
limits: Claims are bound to the tested feed formulation and the tested dryer.
prose:
Powder moisture from the spray dryer fell as inlet air temperature rose, and the driest powder came from the hottest run in the test set. The runs held an inlet air temperature of 180 degrees Celsius with an outlet air temperature of 85 degrees Celsius at the chamber exit. Feed solids content held at 40 percent throughout the runs, and the feed formulation stayed fixed across the temperature steps. Powder moisture, the mass of water per unit mass of wet powder leaving the dryer expressed as a percentage, reached 3.2 percent at the hottest setting. The specification limit, the maximum powder moisture accepted for the product grade under test, stood at 4.0 percent, and the hottest run cleared the limit with margin. At an inlet air temperature of 160 degrees Celsius, powder moisture stood at 4.6 percent, above the specification limit. The moisture change between the two settings tracks the drying capacity of the air stream, and the chamber walls showed no wet deposits at the hotter setting.

Production rate held at 250 kilograms per hour across the runs, and the atomiser speed stayed at the setting used for the earlier development work. Moisture values are means over 12 batches sampled at the chamber outlet, and the spread of the batch values was 0.3 percent. The spread of a moisture value is the standard deviation of the batch values within a run set. Powder from the hotter run flowed freely from the collection vessel, and caking in storage bags was absent from the samples inspected after cooling. Claims are bound to the tested feed formulation and the tested dryer, and other formulations with different solids behaviour stand outside the run set. Powder sampled at the cyclone outlet matched the chamber samples in moisture, and the exhaust air carried no visible plume of wet product during the hotter runs. The moisture gradient across the chamber, from the atomiser to the wall, narrows as the inlet temperature rises, and the wall deposit thins with the gradient.

points: Corrosion rate in seawater reached 0.38 millimetres per year.
Corrosion rate in brackish water reached 0.21 millimetres per year.
Exposure lasted 90 days in each water.
Each condition held 9 coupons.
Both waters were held at 25 degrees Celsius.
Coated coupons in seawater corroded at 0.05 millimetres per year, a reduction of 87 percent against the uncoated seawater rate.
The spread of the coupon rates within a condition was 0.04 millimetres per year.
definitions: corrosion rate = thickness loss per unit time, computed from coupon mass loss and coupon surface area
coupon = flat steel test specimen of fixed dimensions exposed in the test water
spread of a coupon rate = standard deviation of the coupon values within a condition
limits: Claims are bound to the tested waters and the tested temperature; the mass-loss rate averages over the coupon surface and does not state a localised pitting depth.
prose:
Steel corrosion proceeded faster in seawater than in brackish water across the full exposure, and the coating cut the seawater rate by a wide margin. The corrosion rate in seawater, the thickness loss per unit time computed from coupon mass loss and coupon surface area, reached 0.38 millimetres per year. The corrosion rate in brackish water reached 0.21 millimetres per year under the same exposure schedule. Exposure lasted 90 days in each water, and each condition held 9 coupons suspended clear of the tank walls. Both waters were held at 25 degrees Celsius, and aeration followed the same daily pattern in the two tanks. A coupon is a flat steel test specimen of fixed dimensions exposed in the test water, and mass loss was measured after the corrosion product was stripped under the standard cleaning procedure.

Coated coupons in seawater corroded at 0.05 millimetres per year, a reduction of 87 percent against the uncoated seawater rate. The coating surface stayed intact over most of each coated coupon, and attack concentrated at the cut edges where the steel lay exposed. The spread of the coupon rates within a condition was 0.04 millimetres per year, and the spread of a coupon rate is the standard deviation of the coupon values within that condition. Claims are bound to the tested waters and the tested temperature. The mass-loss rate averages over the coupon surface, and the rate does not state a localised pitting depth for either water. Coupon surfaces in seawater carried a loose rust layer over a darker adherent film, and the brackish coupons carried the film alone over most of the surface. Attack at the coupon edges ran deeper than attack at the faces in both waters, and the edge zone is excluded from the area used in the rate calculation, which is computed on the flat faces. The tanks shared a single water supply line and a single temperature controller, and coupon positions rotated at each inspection, distributing any position effect across the conditions.

points: Feed rate of 100 moles per hour with a feed mole fraction of 0.45 for the volatile component.
Target distillate mole fraction of 0.95 and bottoms mole fraction of 0.05.
The overall balance gives a distillate flow of 44.4 moles per hour and a bottoms flow of 55.6 moles per hour.
Reflux ratio set at 2.5.
Relative volatility taken as constant at 2.4 across the column.
The construction gives 11 theoretical stages.
The feed enters on stage 6, counted from the top of the column.
The feed is a saturated liquid, and the q value is 1.
definitions: mole fraction = moles of the volatile component per mole of mixture
reflux ratio = liquid returned to the column per unit of distillate withdrawn
relative volatility = measure of the separation between the two components, from the ratio of their vapour-liquid distribution ratios
theoretical stage = contact stage that brings the passing vapour and liquid streams to equilibrium
q value = thermal condition parameter of the feed, fixed by the fraction of the feed that joins the liquid stream below the feed stage
limits: The construction holds for a binary mixture at constant relative volatility and constant molar overflow.
prose:
The goal of the construction is a stage count for a binary distillation at a stated reflux ratio, and the outcome comes first: the construction gives 11 theoretical stages for the separation specified below. You need the feed rate, the three compositions, the reflux ratio, and a relative volatility before any line is drawn. The feed rate is 100 moles per hour with a feed mole fraction of 0.45 for the volatile component, where the mole fraction is the moles of the volatile component per mole of mixture. The target distillate mole fraction is 0.95 and the bottoms mole fraction is 0.05. The overall balance gives a distillate flow of 44.4 moles per hour and a bottoms flow of 55.6 moles per hour, and the two product flows sum to the feed flow, which is the first check on the arithmetic.

Set the reflux ratio at 2.5, the liquid returned to the column per unit of distillate withdrawn. Take the relative volatility as constant at 2.4 across the column; relative volatility is the measure of the separation between the two components, from the ratio of their vapour-liquid distribution ratios. Draw the equilibrium curve from the volatility, then the rectifying line from the reflux ratio and the distillate composition, then the stripping line through the bottoms composition. The feed is a saturated liquid, and the q value is 1; the q value is the thermal condition parameter of the feed, fixed by the fraction of the feed that joins the liquid stream below the feed stage, and a saturated liquid gives a vertical feed line. Step off stages between the operating lines and the equilibrium curve, starting at the distillate end. A theoretical stage is a contact stage that brings the passing vapour and liquid streams to equilibrium. The feed enters on stage 6, counted from the top of the column. Count the stages from the top throughout: a count started at the bottom misplaces the feed stage and shifts every stage boundary in the enriching section. The construction holds for a binary mixture at constant relative volatility and constant molar overflow.

points: Upstream pipe diameter of 0.20 metres and throat diameter of 0.10 metres.
The area ratio between the upstream section and the throat is 4.
Upstream velocity of 1.5 metres per second.
Continuity gives a throat velocity of 6.0 metres per second.
Water density of 1000 kilograms per cubic metre.
The square of the throat velocity is 36 square metres per square second, and the square of the upstream velocity is 2.25 square metres per square second.
Half the density is 500 kilograms per cubic metre.
The Bernoulli equation gives a pressure drop of 16.9 kilopascals between the upstream section and the throat.
definitions: Bernoulli equation = statement that the sum of pressure head, velocity head, and elevation head stays constant along a streamline for steady, frictionless flow of an incompressible fluid
continuity = statement that the volume flow rate is the same at every section of a filled pipe
pressure drop = pressure at the upstream section minus pressure at the throat
limits: The result holds for frictionless flow; friction in a real pipe lowers the throat pressure recovery and adds a loss term the example omits.
prose:
The goal of the worked example is the pressure drop between a pipe section and a narrower throat, from the Bernoulli equation and continuity alone. The outcome comes first: the pressure drop is 16.9 kilopascals for the water flow specified below. Gather the inputs before any substitution. The upstream pipe diameter is 0.20 metres and the throat diameter is 0.10 metres. The area ratio between the upstream section and the throat is 4, from the squares of the diameters. The upstream velocity is 1.5 metres per second, and the water density is 1000 kilograms per cubic metre. The pipe centreline is horizontal, and the elevation terms in the equation cancel between the two sections.

Apply continuity first. Continuity is the statement that the volume flow rate is the same at every section of a filled pipe, and continuity gives a throat velocity of 6.0 metres per second: the velocity rises in the same ratio as the area falls. The velocity ratio matching the area ratio is the check on this step, and a mismatch means an area has been computed from a radius in one section and a diameter in the other. Apply the Bernoulli equation next. The Bernoulli equation is the statement that the sum of pressure head, velocity head, and elevation head stays constant along a streamline for steady, frictionless flow of an incompressible fluid. The square of the throat velocity is 36 square metres per square second, and the square of the upstream velocity is 2.25 square metres per square second. Half the density is 500 kilograms per cubic metre, and the product of that half density with the difference of the squared velocities gives the pressure drop, the pressure at the upstream section minus the pressure at the throat. Read the warning before the result is used: the calculation holds for frictionless flow, and friction in a real pipe adds a loss term the example omits.

points: Design flow of 60 cubic metres per hour of oil.
Available pressure drop across the valve of 200 kilopascals, equal to 2 bar.
Specific gravity of the oil of 0.85.
The sizing equation gives a required flow coefficient of 39.1.
A catalogue valve with a rated flow coefficient of 50 is selected.
Verification gives a pressure drop of 1.22 bar at the design flow through the selected valve.
definitions: flow coefficient = flow of water, in cubic metres per hour, that passes through the fully open valve at a pressure drop of one bar
specific gravity = density of the process fluid divided by the density of water
rated flow coefficient = flow coefficient of the fully open valve, as listed by the manufacturer
limits: The sizing holds for turbulent flow of a liquid with the stated specific gravity; flashing and cavitation stand outside the calculation.
prose:
The goal of the sizing is a catalogue control valve that passes the design flow at the available pressure drop, with travel margin in hand. The outcome comes first in kind: a standard catalogue valve rated one step above the computed requirement covers the duty, and the steps below give the numbers. You need the design flow, the available pressure drop, and the specific gravity of the fluid before the sizing equation is touched. The design flow is 60 cubic metres per hour of oil. The available pressure drop across the valve is 200 kilopascals, equal to 2 bar, after the line and exchanger losses are subtracted from the pump head. The specific gravity of the oil is 0.85, the density of the process fluid divided by the density of water.

Apply the sizing equation with the pressure drop in bar. The flow coefficient is the flow of water, in cubic metres per hour, that passes through the fully open valve at a pressure drop of one bar, and the sizing equation gives a required flow coefficient of 39.1 for the duty. Select the catalogue valve with a rated flow coefficient of 50; the rated flow coefficient is the flow coefficient of the fully open valve, as listed by the manufacturer. Check the selection before the valve is ordered: the pressure drop at the design flow through the selected valve is 1.22 bar, below the available drop, and the unused head is the margin that keeps the valve off its seat stops at the design point. Read the warning at the point of risk: a valve sized against the full available drop has no head left for fouling in the line, and a fouled line then starves the valve at flows the calculation covers. The sizing holds for turbulent flow of a liquid with the stated specific gravity, and flashing and cavitation stand outside the calculation. Keep the sizing sheet with the valve datasheet: the next sizing on the same line starts from the recorded duty, and a changed duty is sized from the new flow and the new available drop.

points: A coated electrode ran at a cell voltage of 1.72 volts at a current density of 2.0 amperes per square centimetre.
The uncoated baseline electrode ran at 1.85 volts at the same current density.
Energy consumption reached 47 kilowatt hours per kilogram of hydrogen, against 51 kilowatt hours per kilogram for the baseline.
The energy reduction is 7.8 percent.
Faradaic efficiency held at 96 percent.
A durability run lasted 500 hours at the stated current density.
definitions: cell voltage = voltage across one electrolysis cell at the stated current density
current density = current passed per unit of electrode area
faradaic efficiency = measured hydrogen output divided by the hydrogen output the passed charge could produce at most
energy consumption = electrical energy supplied per kilogram of hydrogen produced
prose: Hydrogen production by water electrolysis carries an energy cost set mainly by the cell voltage, and electrode coatings that lower the voltage at a working current density are a direct route to a lower cost. A coated electrode was tested in a membrane electrolysis cell against an uncoated baseline electrode of the same geometry. The coated electrode ran at a cell voltage of 1.72 volts at a current density of 2.0 amperes per square centimetre, where the cell voltage is the voltage across one electrolysis cell and the current density is the current passed per unit of electrode area. The uncoated baseline electrode ran at 1.85 volts at the same current density. Energy consumption, the electrical energy supplied per kilogram of hydrogen produced, reached 47 kilowatt hours per kilogram for the coated electrode, against 51 kilowatt hours per kilogram for the baseline, an energy reduction of 7.8 percent. Faradaic efficiency, the measured hydrogen output divided by the hydrogen output the passed charge could produce at most, held at 96 percent. A durability run lasted 500 hours at the stated current density with the voltage advantage retained. The coating lowers the electrical cost of electrolytic hydrogen at the tested scale, and the result supports coating development for larger cells.

points: Median granule size reached 420 micrometres, against 310 micrometres for the baseline granulation.
Tablet tensile strength reached 2.1 megapascals, against 1.6 megapascals for the baseline.
Binder solution was added at 18 percent of the dry powder mass.
Disintegration time held at 6 minutes.
Values are means over 5 batches; the spread of the median granule size was 25 micrometres.
definitions: median granule size = granule size at which half the sample mass is finer and half is coarser
tensile strength = breaking force of a tablet converted to a stress from the tablet dimensions
disintegration time = time for a tablet to break apart in the test fluid under the standard test motion
spread of the median granule size = standard deviation of the batch median values
prose: Wet granulation sets the size of pharmaceutical granules, and granule size governs the strength and disintegration of the tablets pressed from the granules. A high-shear granulation with a staged binder addition was tested against a single-shot baseline granulation of the same formulation. Median granule size, the granule size at which half the sample mass is finer and half is coarser, reached 420 micrometres, against 310 micrometres for the baseline granulation. Tablet tensile strength, the breaking force of a tablet converted to a stress from the tablet dimensions, reached 2.1 megapascals, against 1.6 megapascals for the baseline. Binder solution was added at 18 percent of the dry powder mass in both routes. Disintegration time, the time for a tablet to break apart in the test fluid under the standard test motion, held at 6 minutes for the staged route. Values are means over 5 batches, and the spread of the median granule size was 25 micrometres, the standard deviation of the batch median values. Staged binder addition gives coarser granules and stronger tablets at an unchanged disintegration time, and the route offers a formulation lever that does not trade strength against disintegration.

points: The production well delivers water at 78 degrees Celsius from a depth of 900 metres.
Network supply temperature is 65 degrees Celsius and return temperature is 38 degrees Celsius, a difference of 27 degrees Celsius.
Network flow is 40 litres per second.
Thermal capacity of the scheme is 4.5 megawatts.
The scheme serves 1200 homes.
definitions: supply temperature = temperature of the water sent into the district network
return temperature = temperature of the water coming back from the district network
thermal capacity = heat delivery rate of the scheme at the stated temperatures and flow
limits: The study covers one heating season of operation.
prose:
District heating from a geothermal well serves a housing district in the study area, and the scheme has run through one heating season under metered operation. The production well delivers water at 78 degrees Celsius from a depth of 900 metres. Network supply temperature, the temperature of the water sent into the district network, is 65 degrees Celsius, and return temperature, the temperature of the water coming back from the district network, is 38 degrees Celsius, a difference of 27 degrees Celsius. Network flow is 40 litres per second at the design point, and thermal capacity, the heat delivery rate of the scheme at the stated temperatures and flow, is 4.5 megawatts. The scheme serves 1200 homes.

Geothermal district schemes elsewhere have published supply performance in detail, and seasonal output curves are well documented for mature fields. The behaviour of a young field under sustained extraction is the missing piece of knowledge: no published record tracks production temperature and well scaling together across the opening seasons of a scheme of this size, and output forecasts for new schemes rest on reservoir models that the early operating record has not tested. This study assembles the first-season record for the scheme. Production temperature, network temperatures, and flow come from the scheme metering, scaling deposits come from coupons pulled from the production line at the season inspections, and the study compares the measured heat delivery against the design rating across the season.

points: Reactor temperature held at 500 degrees Celsius.
Oil yield reached 62 percent of the feed mass, with char at 18 percent and gas at 20 percent.
Oil water content stood at 1.8 percent.
Oil calorific value reached 38 megajoules per kilogram, against a diesel reference value of 43 megajoules per kilogram.
Feed rate held at 50 kilograms per hour.
definitions: pyrolysis = thermal decomposition of a material in the absence of oxygen
oil yield = mass of condensed oil collected per unit mass of feed
calorific value = heat released per unit mass of fuel on complete combustion
limits: The record covers the mixed feedstock received at the plant during the trial period.
prose:
Pyrolysis of mixed plastic waste at the trial plant converts a low-value feedstock into an oil, a char, and a gas, and the oil fraction carries the economic case for the process. Pyrolysis is the thermal decomposition of a material in the absence of oxygen. Reactor temperature held at 500 degrees Celsius across the trial runs, and feed rate held at 50 kilograms per hour. Oil yield, the mass of condensed oil collected per unit mass of feed, reached 62 percent of the feed mass, with char at 18 percent and gas at 20 percent; the three product shares close the mass balance for the runs. Oil water content stood at 1.8 percent. Oil calorific value, the heat released per unit mass of fuel on complete combustion, reached 38 megajoules per kilogram, against a diesel reference value of 43 megajoules per kilogram.

Published pyrolysis studies rest largely on sorted, single-polymer feeds, and the yields and oil properties of sorted feeds are well documented. Mixed feeds from a collection stream vary in composition from load to load, and the effect of that variation on oil quality is the missing piece of knowledge: no published record links the composition of a mixed feed, load by load, to the water content and calorific value of the oil the feed produces. This study assembles the trial record for the mixed feedstock received at the plant. Feed composition comes from hand sorting of each load, and oil samples from each run go to water content and calorific value measurement under the standard fuel test methods.

points: Obscuration held at 12 percent during measurement.
Particle refractive index set at 1.52 and dispersant refractive index set at 1.33.
Each sample received 5 repeat measurements.
Pump speed held at 2000 revolutions per minute.
Sample mass was 0.5 grams per measurement.
Ultrasound was applied for 60 seconds before measurement.
definitions: obscuration = fraction of the incident laser light removed from the beam by the suspended particles
refractive index = ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in the material
volume median diameter = particle diameter at which half the particle volume is finer
limits: The method covers spherical-equivalent sizing; plate-like and needle-like particles are reported as equivalent spheres.
prose:
Particle size distributions were measured by laser diffraction on a wet dispersion unit, with the size reported as a spherical-equivalent distribution. The sample was dispersed in water in the dispersion unit until the suspension circulated steadily through the measurement cell. Sample mass was 0.5 grams per measurement, weighed on the bench balance beside the instrument. Ultrasound was applied for 60 seconds before measurement, breaking loose agglomerates while the suspension circulated. Pump speed held at 2000 revolutions per minute throughout each measurement, keeping coarse particles suspended without drawing air into the cell. Obscuration, the fraction of the incident laser light removed from the beam by the suspended particles, held at 12 percent during measurement. Where the obscuration rises above the set value during a run, the suspension is diluted before the measurement is taken: a dense suspension scatters light more than once before the light reaches the detector, and multiple scattering shifts the reported distribution toward finer sizes.

The optical model took a particle refractive index of 1.52 and a dispersant refractive index of 1.33, where the refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in the material. A background reading on the clean dispersant preceded each sample, and the sample reading was corrected against that background before the distribution was computed. Each sample received 5 repeat measurements, and the reported distribution is the mean of the repeats. The volume median diameter, the particle diameter at which half the particle volume is finer, is drawn from the reported distribution. The method covers spherical-equivalent sizing, and plate-like and needle-like particles are reported as equivalent spheres. A check sample of a reference powder ran at the start of each session, and a drift in the reference distribution stopped the session until the cell windows were cleaned and the alignment repeated.

points: Titrant acid concentration was 0.1 moles per litre.
Sample volume was 50 millilitres.
The titration endpoint was a pH of 4.5.
Each sample received 3 replicate titrations.
A standard check solution of 250 milligrams per litre gave a recovery of 98 percent.
definitions: alkalinity = acid-neutralising capacity of a water sample, stated as milligrams per litre of calcium carbonate equivalent
endpoint = pH at which the titration is stopped and the titre is read
titre = volume of titrant delivered from the burette at the endpoint
limits: The method covers samples titrated promptly after collection; stored samples with biological activity stand outside the procedure.
prose:
Alkalinity was measured by titration of the water sample with standard acid to a fixed endpoint, with the result stated as milligrams per litre of calcium carbonate equivalent. Alkalinity is the acid-neutralising capacity of a water sample. The titrant acid concentration was 0.1 moles per litre, standardised against dried sodium carbonate before the sample set was run. Sample volume was 50 millilitres, delivered by pipette into a conical flask with a measured addition of indicator solution. The titration endpoint was a pH of 4.5, read on the bench pH meter rather than by the indicator colour alone; the endpoint is the pH at which the titration is stopped and the titre is read, and the titre is the volume of titrant delivered from the burette at the endpoint. Acid was added slowly near the endpoint with the flask swirled continuously. Where the endpoint is passed before the reading is taken, the titration is discarded and the sample is titrated again: an overshot endpoint inflates the titre, and no correction recovers the discarded run.

Each sample received 3 replicate titrations, and the reported alkalinity is the mean of the replicates. A blank titration on the dilution water preceded each sample set, and the blank titre was subtracted from every sample titre before the calculation. Alkalinity was computed from the corrected titre, the acid concentration, and the sample volume, with the equivalent mass of calcium carbonate as the conversion factor. A standard check solution of 250 milligrams per litre gave a recovery of 98 percent across the study, and a failed check stopped sample work until the acid was restandardised. The method covers samples titrated promptly after collection, and stored samples with biological activity stand outside the procedure.

points: The trial ran for 6 months on the works wastewater.
Influent chemical oxygen demand averaged 400 milligrams per litre.
Effluent chemical oxygen demand averaged 28 milligrams per litre, against a discharge limit of 40 milligrams per litre.
Removal of chemical oxygen demand reached 93 percent.
Membrane flux held at 18 litres per square metre per hour.
The cleaning interval stretched to 45 days by the end of the trial.
Energy consumption stood at 0.9 kilowatt hours per cubic metre treated.
definitions: chemical oxygen demand = mass of oxygen equivalent to the oxidisable matter in a litre of water
membrane flux = volume of treated water passing through a unit of membrane area in a unit of time
removal = influent concentration minus effluent concentration, divided by the influent concentration
limits: The claim is bound to the tested wastewater and the tested season; cold-weather operation and membrane ageing beyond the trial duration stand outside the record.
prose:
The membrane bioreactor met the discharge limit across the trial at the tested loading, and the trial record supports the reactor at the scale and the wastewater tested. The trial ran for 6 months on the works wastewater. Influent chemical oxygen demand, the mass of oxygen equivalent to the oxidisable matter in a litre of water, averaged 400 milligrams per litre. Effluent chemical oxygen demand averaged 28 milligrams per litre, against a discharge limit of 40 milligrams per litre, and removal of chemical oxygen demand reached 93 percent. Removal is the influent concentration minus the effluent concentration, divided by the influent concentration. Membrane flux, the volume of treated water passing through a unit of membrane area in a unit of time, held at 18 litres per square metre per hour, and the cleaning interval stretched to 45 days by the end of the trial as the aeration control settled. Energy consumption stood at 0.9 kilowatt hours per cubic metre treated.

The claim is bound to the tested wastewater and the tested season. Cold-weather operation stands outside the record, and membrane ageing beyond the trial duration is untested: flux stability across the trial does not state flux stability across a membrane service life. Effluent quality at higher loadings than the tested loading is likewise outside the claim. Sludge wasting from the reactor followed the effluent record, and the wasted sludge thickened without the bulking that the earlier activated sludge plant on the site had shown in wet weather. The trial plant shared the works inlet screen and grit removal with the main treatment stream, and the membrane trains took the screened flow directly.

prose: Thermogravimetric curve of the polymer blend under nitrogen. Samples of 10 milligrams were heated at 20 degrees Celsius per minute under a nitrogen flow of 50 millilitres per minute. The curve shown is the mean of 3 replicate runs. The first mass-loss step begins at an onset temperature of 285 degrees Celsius and removes 45 percent of the sample mass; the second step begins at 340 degrees Celsius. Residue at 600 degrees Celsius is 6 percent of the sample mass. Onset temperatures carry a spread of 4 degrees Celsius across the replicates, and onsets were fixed by the tangent intersection method on each replicate curve.

definitions: rate constant = proportionality factor between the reaction rate and the reactant concentration
pre-exponential factor = frequency factor in the Arrhenius statement, carrying the units of the rate constant
activation energy = energy barrier in the Arrhenius statement
gas constant = constant linking energy and absolute temperature in the Arrhenius statement
absolute temperature = temperature measured from absolute zero

prose:
The rate constant is the proportionality factor between the reaction rate and the reactant concentration, and the constant carries units of per second for the first-order reaction under study. Temperature dependence of the rate constant follows the Arrhenius statement. The statement gives the rate constant as the pre-exponential factor multiplied by an exponential term, the exponential of minus the activation energy divided by the product of the gas constant and the absolute temperature. In the statement, A is the pre-exponential factor carrying the units of the rate constant, Ea is the activation energy, R is the gas constant with a value of 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin, and T is the absolute temperature measured from absolute zero. The statement holds where a single mechanism controls the rate; below 280 kelvin a second mechanism contributes to the measured rate in the system under study, and the statement does not cover that range.

The exponential term sets the temperature sensitivity of the constant. A higher activation energy steepens the rise of the rate constant with temperature, and the pre-exponential factor shifts the whole curve without changing the steepness. Rate constants for the worked example come from concentration decay curves recorded at each test temperature, with the constant taken from the slope of the logarithmic decay. For an activation energy of 25000 joules per mole, the measured rate constant at 300 kelvin is 0.004 per second. The statement predicts a ratio of 1.87 between the rate constants at the two test temperatures, and the predicted rate constant at 320 kelvin is 0.0075 per second. The predicted rise is the check on the activation energy drawn from the decay curves: a measured rise far from the predicted ratio marks a change of mechanism or a temperature error in the reactor, and either fault invalidates the single-mechanism reading of the curve.
